items.title: 接入多款第三方模型，豆包工作也模型自由了
items.description: 头图来源：豆包工作官网 豆包工作也模型自由了。 11 月 12 日，豆包工作宣布接入 Kimi K3.1 Pro、GLM 5.3、DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 等多款第三方模型，支持用户按需选型完成任务。同步在模型选择页面标注各模型额度消耗倍率，倍率越低消耗越少，便于用户结合任务需求与使用成本做决策。 同时平台推出两项限时优惠：一是工作日及节假日的指定时段内，使用活动模型可享受额度消耗折扣；二是豆包 2.1 Lite、DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 两款模型限时下调额度消耗倍率，同等任务消耗额度更少。 一、补全多模型，解决「有的选」 本轮更新中，豆包工作一次性接入 Kimi 3.1 Pro、GLM 5.3、DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 三款第三方模型，进一步补齐了模型能力矩阵。 具体来看，三款模型各有侧重，可以分别对应企业不同层级的工作场景：Kimi 3.1 Pro 主打百万字级超长上下文处理能力；GLM 5.3 侧重中文语言理解与生成；DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 以高响应速度和高性价比为核心，定位轻量日常任务。 加上此前已经开放的第三方模型，以及字节跳动自研的豆包 2.1、豆包 2.1 Lite 等主力模型，豆包工作已经具备了覆盖「高端能力型、均衡通用型、轻量效率型」三个层级的模型矩阵。 不同能力、不同定价的模型相互补充，基本可以覆盖企业从核心复杂任务到日常基础工作的多场景 AI 需求。 事实上，豆包工作此前就已向企业客户开放第三方模型能力。本轮扩容并非单纯的数量叠加，而是基于企业真实工作流的场景化补全。 图片来源：豆包工作官网 此外，我们也注意到，豆包工作本次同步更新了 LOGO，大家熟悉的豆包形象就此「持证上岗」，进入了专业办公场景。 二、额度倍率透明化，把成本决策权交还给用户 如果说模型扩容是解决「有没有得选」的问题，那么额度消耗倍率的透明化标注，则是解决「选得明不明白」的问题。 在当前的企业级 AI 市场，成本不透明是很多企业的普遍困扰。不同模型的计费规则各不相同，有的按输入输出 token 计费，有的按调用次数收费，不同单位之间换算复杂，普通用户很难快速判断一款模型的实际使用成本。 很多团队在使用过程中，往往难以预估单任务开销，直到账单出来才发现超出预算，也很难追溯成本的具体构成。 针对这一问题，豆包工作在模型选择页面统一标注了各模型的额度消耗倍率—— 倍率系数越低，同等任务消耗的平台额度越少。所有模型的消耗标准统一到同一额度体系下，用户选型时可直观对比成本差异，结合任务优先级与预算快速决策，也便于企业做部门的成本管控。 在简单小额任务免费的基础上，豆包工作同步上线两项限时优惠政策，进一步压低使用成本： 一是指定时段折扣，工作日及节假日的优惠时段内使用活动模型，可享受额度消耗减免，兼顾用户成本与平台算力效率； 二是高频模型降倍率，针对豆包 2.1 Lite 与 DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 两款日常高频使用的轻量模型，限时下调消耗倍率，同等任务消耗更少，提升全员日常使用的额度耐用性。 当大模型的基础能力逐渐拉平，如何帮企业把 AI 用起来、用得划算，才是落地的关键。从提供单一模型，到提供多模型矩阵；从黑盒计费，到透明化成本管控，豆包工作的产品迭代路径，契合了企业 AI 从「尝鲜」到「常态化生产工具」的转变趋势。 再往前看一步，当模型足够多、倍率足够清晰，用户可能连「选哪个模型」都不需要亲自操心，平台基于任务类型自动路由、智能调度，会成为下一个自然的产品方向。

items.description: 11 月 4 日，混元 Hy4 正式发布，模型权重将在近期开源，主打性价比的轻量版 Hy4 flash 也一起亮相。腾讯给它的定位是——首次跻身最强开源模型之列。 过去一年，腾讯在 AI 上最多被人看见的，是 WorkBuddy 这类 Agent 和应用产品；到了更底层的模型上，它的声量明显弱于应用。Hy4 真正要回答的，是腾讯在模型这条线上的身位。

items.description: 11 月 9 日消息，英伟达 CEO 黄仁勋当地时间 8 日于公司官网发布致全员公开信，就个人私事致歉，同时披露董事会将针对相关报道提及的国家安全关切展开独立调查。 黄仁勋在信中承认自己对妻子不忠，坦言该行为伤害家人，对此承担全部责任，并接受外界批评。他表示家人不应为其个人选择负责，恳请公众给予家人隐私空间，希望能有机会重新赢回家人信任。他强调自己对英伟达始终坚定，将努力重新赢得团队与投资方的信赖。

items.title: 为什么「陪伴」，注定是 Personal AI 的核心
items.description: 最近这一波 Personal AI 实在太火了，我也注册了一个 Muse 体验了一下。 整个体验下来，我感觉 Muse 的能力实在一般，远没到让人惊叹的地步。但奇怪的是，它确实带来了一种真切的陪伴感。这种陪伴感，甚至直接改变了我的使用习惯，让我总是忍不住想找它聊聊，哪怕只是把最琐碎的需求丢给它。

items.title: 创业者做 Personal Agent，有没有一线生机？
items.description: 最近一阶段，Personal Agent 很热。有趣的是，这个概念迅速火爆又迅速有了一个共识，几波讨论下来大家的观点似乎是： Personal Agent 的机会是大厂的，创业者基本没戏。 虽然一般情况下，「入口级机会归大厂」确实是大概率发生的事情，但 Personal Agent 真的是个「入口」的问题吗？真的意味着「这件事里没有创业者的位置」吗？

items.title: 收购 EA 后，银湖资本与沙特基金 250 亿美元报价 Unity；超10万款应用已适配iPhone Duo；美国再发生 NVIDIA AI 设备失窃案
items.description: 据路透社援引未具名知情人士的消息报道，由美国私募股权公司银湖资本（Silver Lake Partners）与沙特阿拉伯主权财富基金——公共投资基金（PIF）组成的投资者财团，已向 Unity Software 提出收购要约，对这家公司的估值约为 250 亿美元。据悉，Unity 正在认真考虑这一报价，并已聘请一家投资银行提供咨询。 据路透社援引未具名知情人士的消息报道，由美国私募股权公司银湖资本（Silver Lake Partners）与沙特阿拉伯主权财富基金——公共投资基金（PIF）组成的投资者财团，已向 Unity Software 提出收购要约，对这家公司的估值约为 250 亿美元。据悉，Unity 正在认真考虑这一报价，并已聘请一家投资银行提供咨询。（来源：cnBeta）

items.title: 办公提效之后，企业级 Agent 开始对经营结果负责
items.description: 从查资料、写文档到处理日常办公事务，桌面办公智能体完成了第一轮普及，办公提效的价值已经成为行业共识。但当 AI 进一步走向企业核心业务，搭出一个智能体不难，难的是让它真正跑进业务流程，适配复杂的系统、权限与规则，持续产出可量化的经营价值。 在腾讯云副总裁吴永坚看来，未来企业级智能体的核心赛道，对话式的桌面办公 Agent 和服务经营的 Service Agent 会是两个长期并行的赛道。大模型提供了理解与推理能力，但想让 AI 真正参与业务经营，还需要一套能够打通系统、管好权限、支撑长期稳定运行的企业级平台。

items.title: 马斯克官宣 Cybertruck 停产：销量不足预期一成；李飞飞团队推出世界模型「模拟掌机」；小米汽车成立国际事业部｜极客早知道
items.description: 11 月 6 日消息，特斯拉 CEO 马斯克在社交平台 X 发文表示，公司将于明年年中前后，逐步收尾得州超级工厂的 Cybertruck 电动皮卡生产，为 Cybercab 车型扩产腾出产能空间。 Cybertruck 首席工程师随后回应称，Cybertruck 是特斯拉研发新技术的重要载体，其线控转向等技术已应用于 Cybercab，产品技术生命将在新车型上延续。

items.title: 浙大彭思达：从元宇宙到具身智能，一个三维视觉研究者的八年 | 世界模型50人
items.description: 传统MV拍摄，摄影机架在哪里，观众看到的就是哪个角度。现在用多台摄像机同时记录舞者动作，再重建出一个三维动态场景，镜头可以任意调换位置；从队形正面绕到侧面，穿过舞者之间，甚至换一个从未真正架设过的机位，重新观看刚才的表演。 今年10月，韩国SM娱乐创始人李秀满在新女团A2O LITE的出道活动上，展示了这项名为4D Gaussian Splatting（4DGS）的技术。

items.title: 中金公司与蚂蚁集团达成战略合作 共探AI赋能财富管理
items.description: 11月13日，中国国际金融股份有限公司（简称“中金公司”）与蚂蚁科技集团股份有限公司（简称“蚂蚁集团”）签署战略合作协议。 双方将结合中金公司在专业投研、金融服务等方面的积累，以及蚂蚁集团在人工智能、行业生态、客户运营等方面的优势，围绕金融大模型技术创新、AI赋能财富管理、客户全生命周期服务等领域开展合作，共同探索“AI+金融”创新路径。 中金公司党委副书记、副董事长、总裁王曙光（右二），蚂蚁集团首席执行官、蚂蚁数科董事长韩歆毅（左二）出席并见证签约仪式。中金公司党委委员、中金财富党委书记、总裁王建力（右一），蚂蚁集团资深副总裁、蚂蚁数科CEO赵闻飙（左一）代表双方签署协议。 随着大模型和智能体技术发展，AI正逐步深入投研、客户服务和财富管理等金融环节。根据协议，双方将重点围绕三个方向开展合作。 一是探索AI赋能财富管理人机协同工作新模式。 双方计划探索打造服务与营销协同的智能体集群，将AI应用于客户需求洞察、资产配置、投资研究等环节，辅助财富管理顾问提升服务效率和专业能力，为客户提供更及时、个性化的服务，推动财富管理从“被动响应”向“主动服务”转变。 二是探索全域客户价值全周期经营体系建设。 双方拟共建覆盖客户全生命周期的精细化财富经营体系。通过智能客户陪伴、精准需求洞察与买方投顾专业服务，提升客户满意度和长期粘性；通过AI辅助客户需求分析与服务匹配，探索更便捷、个性化的财富管理服务，满足客户不同人生阶段需求。 三是深化智能技术和模型合作。 双方将围绕智能体评测基准建设，在投研研判、财务文本解析、估值建模等场景开展技术验证，推动AI技术安全、可靠地应用于实际业务。 双方还计划在投资者教育、专业研究内容、市场观点分享等领域开展合作，探索更多专业金融知识与服务触达用户的方式。 中金公司党委副书记、副董事长、总裁王曙光表示，人工智能为金融服务创新带来新机遇。中金公司始终重视专业能力建设与客户长期价值，希望通过此次合作，将金融专业优势与蚂蚁集团技术及平台能力相结合，探索AI在投研、财富管理等业务中的应用，更好满足客户多元化金融服务需求。 蚂蚁集团首席执行官、蚂蚁数科董事长韩歆毅表示，AI在金融行业的价值不仅是提升金融机构效率，更重要的是让客户获得更好的服务体验。期待与中金公司共同探索大模型和智能体在金融业务中的应用，让AI更好辅助专业人员工作，让金融服务更懂客户、更便捷、更有温度。 此次合作将进一步结合双方在金融专业服务、人工智能技术及平台生态方面的优势，探索AI在财富管理领域的实际应用，为提升金融服务效率、改善客户体验提供实践经验。 关于中金公司 中国国际金融股份有限公司成立于1995年，是中国领先的投资银行和综合金融服务机构，业务涵盖投资银行、股票业务、固定收益、资产管理、私募股权及财富管理等领域，致力于为客户提供高质量金融服务。 关于蚂蚁集团 蚂蚁集团起步于2004年诞生的支付宝，以“构建服务业数字化基础设施”为愿景，专注于科技应用和普惠服务，希望用科技为世界带来微小而美好的改变。 近年来，蚂蚁集团持续布局人工智能技术，在大模型、智能体及可信AI等领域开展创新，推动AI技术在金融及生活服务等场景应用。 雷峰网 雷峰网

items.title: 40 亿参数模型拿下 6 个评测第一，西湖大学团队押注「概念世界模型」
items.description: 海外李飞飞、Yann LeCun 等学术大佬亲自下场，国内极佳视界、逆矩阵、流形空间等创业公司高密度入场。 但最近几个月，入场的力量开始发生变化，下场的不再只是公司，高校和地方政府也开始组织力量，参与这场技术竞争。

items.title: 中大梁小丹团队，GeoThinker 两项研究成果，破除空间推理「几何信息用不好、计算开销大」难题
items.description: 判断物体的位置、距离和空间关系，是视觉语言模型实现空间推理需要具备的能力。现在一种常见做法，是接入 VGGT 这类三维几何编码器，从多视角图像中提取深度、点云等空间线索，辅助模型判断。 但外部几何信息并不是越多越好。 无关的几何特征可能干扰模型判断，每次调用外部三维模型，也会增加推理时间。

items.title: 京博控股集团与千问办公达成战略合作，共创化工行业AI Native标杆
items.description: 近日，京博控股集团与千问办公达成战略合作，明确全集团将基于千问办公打造AI Native组织。后续双方将围绕科研创新、生产运营优化、经营分析、流程组织重构等核心场景展开合作，共同探索化工行业的智能化升级路径。京博控股集团执行董事、首席轮值总裁栾波，集团轮值总裁兼海外总裁汪君华和千问办公CEO陈宇森等共同出席了本次战略合作签约仪式。 图示 京博控股集团和千问办公战略合作签约现场 京博控股集团是中国500强企业，向全球50余个国家和地区提供高性能新材料、高端化学品、高端装备智造、数智化解决方案与安环能碳配套服务系统。依托千问办公，京博将在化工、新材料等核心生产场景，探索用Agent重塑流程架构，实现增收提效；另一方面，京博将借助千问办公沉淀管理经验，提升公司整体运营效率。 栾波表示，基于千问办公的能力，期待双方能够在研发、生产、组织管理上优化创新，共同打造化工行业AI Native标杆企业。 据悉，千问办公是阿里巴巴旗下企业级通用Agent产品，是AI办公赛道增长最快的产品之一，目前行业头部企业均已接入千问办公。

items.title: 独家丨腾讯 AI 李牧青离职，出任 AI 公司联席 CEO
items.description: 雷峰网独家获悉，近日，腾讯云 AI 全球业务负责人李牧青，正式出任教育 AI 科技公司启鸣达人联席 CEO。 雷峰网了解到，李牧青本科、硕士毕业于上海交通大学，曾任 UCLA 访问学者。2016 年，他加入依图科技，主导早期 AI 产业化体系的建设，亲历「AI 四小龙」从初创走向鼎盛。 2018 年，李牧青加入腾讯优图，出任首席方案架构师，负责计算机视觉技术的落地。此后分别担任腾讯云智能总架构师、腾讯云智能副总经理、腾讯云 AI 全球业务负责人。在腾讯期间，他带领团队在二十多个行业的一线推进大模型与 AI 落地，从零搭建海外业务，推动 AI 产品与解决方案深度契合当地需求，实现本地化。 他于今年九月正式离开腾讯，随后出任教育 AI 科技公司启鸣达人联席 CEO。 一位 AI 资深从业者告诉雷峰网，90 年前后出生的李牧青，是少有完整经历过巅峰 AI 四小龙、大厂计算机视觉实验室、大模型商业化落地和海外市场开拓时期的青年 AI 落地领军人物，此次出任教育 AI 科技公司启鸣达人联席 CEO，或许能为教育行业带来些许不一样的创新。 雷峰网

items.description: Nvidia's ousted CEO Jensen Huang's downfall isn’t just your run-of-the-mill salacious billionaire sex scandal. He was using his influence to push the AI industry in some very specific ways.

items.title: Jensen Huang's ouster likely traces back to Nvidia's risky business practices more than his personal life
items.description: Jensen Huang likely left Nvidia more because of risky business practices than anything else, a Wall Street Journal report suggests. At the very least, those practices made him enemies internally. The company offered cloud providers billions in financial guarantees for chip purchases, including a planned $250 billion deal with OpenAI. Interim CEO and then-CFO Colette Kress tried to contain the risk, and Huang reportedly didn't like that.

items.title: OpenAI rebuilt AI shopping from scratch with ChatGPT Wallet
items.description: OpenAI is taking a second shot at AI-powered shopping with ChatGPT Wallet after scrapping its first approach, Instant Checkout. Users register a card once and confirm each purchase through Face ID or a fingerprint, while actual card details stay hidden behind payment tokens. Rivals such as Anthropic, Meta, and xAI already have their agents making purchases.

items.title: Banks bar Chinese and Hong Kong investors from Anthropic IPO over US export controls
items.description: Chinese investors are shut out of Anthropic's IPO, Bloomberg reports. Banks are rejecting buy orders from mainland China and Hong Kong, citing U.S. export control rules known as ITAR. Similar restrictions applied during SpaceX's IPO, and Anthropic's products aren't available in either region anyway.

items.title: Anthropic's Claude for Manufacturing plugs AI directly into factory software to automate industrial workflows
items.description: Anthropic's new Claude for Manufacturing plugin connects the AI directly to Autodesk Fusion, Oracle NetSuite, and Infor. Its 17 specialized skills let the AI draft quotes, compare suppliers, and place backup orders when deliveries are delayed, all after human approval. The plugin doesn't control physical machines yet, but Anthropic is separately developing the Model Hardware Standard for that.

items.title: Nearly 70 percent of US agencies use generative AI, and unions are finally catching up with guardrails
items.description: US public-sector unions are increasingly pushing through protections against AI surveillance and automated firings. In Oakland, a strike vote forced retraining programs instead of layoffs, and a transport union in Ohio won veto power over autonomous vehicles. California banned so-called bossware. All of this is happening while nearly 70 percent of US government agencies already use generative AI.

items.title: Former OpenAI researcher says he found Nvidia Blackwell fingerprints hidden inside six Chinese AI models
items.description: Former OpenAI researcher Will DePue says he has produced the first technical evidence that DeepSeek, Moonshot AI, MiniMax, and Ant Group are using Nvidia's latest Blackwell GPUs despite US export controls. His forensic method reads characteristic chip signatures directly from published model weights. He estimates the hardware behind the five training runs cost more than half a billion dollars.

items.title: Anthropic's IPO is six times oversubscribed and on track to become the largest public offering in history
items.description: Anthropic is on track for the largest IPO ever, with orders exceeding available shares by a factor of six.

items.title: Meta's Muse now calls businesses for you, but many companies might just hang up on the AI
items.description: Meta's AI agent Muse can now call businesses on behalf of paying US subscribers, handling everything from cable providers to restaurants. The agent already has over 10 million users, according to Meta's AI chief Alexandr Wang. Google Gemini, Instinct, and xAI's Grok Bot offer the same feature, but many businesses hang up as soon as they detect an AI on the line.

items.title: Gemini Decisions API
items.description: Gemini Decisions API Google join Jev and OpenAI in the decision model category with "Gemini Decision 1". This new model API is almost identical to Jev: it supports the same three types of questions (yes/no, choice, and rubric-scoring) and even reuses Jev's term "Noul" for a yes/no question. It's priced the same as the GPT-6 Luna decision model: 10 cents per million input tokens, and output is free. Jev remains the cheapest of the three, at 4.2 cents per million. Jev is text (and JSON) only. OpenAI can handle text and images. Gemini Decision 1 is fully multi-model: it covers text, images, audio, video, and PDFs. I tested it against video by passing these questions to it along with my Yonkers stomping robot video file: dragon: Does this video have a dragon in it? robot: Does this video have a robot in it? france: Is this video set in France? usa: Is this video set in the USA? Jev and OpenAI both return 1.0 or 0.0 for yes/no questions, but Gemini insists on being a little less confident than that: { "dragon" : { "type" : " yes_no " , "probability" : 0.04976021841520312 }, "robot" : { "type" : " yes_no " , "probability" : 0.9234055387792485 }, "france" : { "type" : " yes_no " , "probability" : 0.08329171353166241 }, "usa" : { "type" : " yes_no " , "probability" : 0.9230459995157706 } } Via Hacker News Tags: ai , generative-ai , gemini , llm-release , jev , decision-models

items.title: Anthropic's IPO roadshow video
items.description: Anthropic's IPO roadshow video Anthropic kicked off their IPO roadshow yesterday, and their roadshow video has some previously unreleased information about how their business works. The section on "Approach to compute" with co-founder Tom Brown is particularly interesting, describing how Anthropic train and serve Claude across AWS Trainium, Google TPUs, NVIDIA GPUs, and AMD GPUs. I'm not sure why there's no official video transcript, but here's one that I extracted using MacWhisper. Highlights below: We train and serve Claude now across all four major chip families. That's only possible because early on we made an unconventional bet on a multi-chip strategy. At the time, many people thought that running AI models on different chips wasn't worth the effort. Each chip needs its own tailored software stack and inference stack, which is expensive and difficult to build. We've now been doing it for years, and we've gotten incredibly good at it. [...] As an example, this year, we started working with AMD GPUs for the first time. In the past, bringing on a new chip platform took dozens of engineers months of work This time, we had Mythos try it out. It got Claude running on AMD in just three days, with basically no human intervention . Claude ported or wrote almost 100% of the kernels. [...] The second driver of our compute advantage is our rate of discovery of compute multipliers. We focus on total effective compute, which is the multiplicative product of physical capacity times the compute multipliers that we discover. Each one we discover makes our pool of total effective compute bigger. For example, say you need 100 units of compute to train a model of a certain intelligence. A 4x compute multiplier means you can use 25 units of compute to train the exact same model. Or…

items.title: Quoting Prompting Claude Fable 5.2
items.description: Claude Fable 5.2 pays close attention to who owns the code it works on. In Anthropic’s testing on small coding tasks, the model tended to add to the existing structure when the prompt said nothing about ownership or presented the code base as someone else’s, even when that duplicated existing code. When the prompt said the code base was the model’s own, it often consolidated duplicated code and sometimes made related fixes without being asked. If you want the model to improve the structure as it works, say that the code is its own: You are the owner and long-term maintainer of this codebase, and its design is up to you. The ownership sentence makes the model much more likely to consolidate duplicated code into one shared function. In Anthropic’s testing on small coding tasks, the model consolidated duplicated code in under 10 percent of runs without the sentence and in about 75 percent of runs with it. — Prompting Claude Fable 5.2 , Anthropic documentation Tags: ai , prompt-engineering , generative-ai , llms , anthropic , claude-mythos-fable

items.title: llm-anthropic 0.31
items.description: Release: llm-anthropic 0.31 Anthropic released Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 today. Fable 5.2 is currently ranked first on Artificial Analysis . Anthropic say it "solved two open problems in the physics of black holes", so clearly their internal benchmarks have become more ambitious! I've added the new models to llm-anthropic , so you can now run prompts through Fable 5.2 like this: uv tool install llm llm install llm-anthropic llm keys set anthropic # paste key here llm -m claude-fable-5.2 "Generate an SVG of a pelican riding a bicycle" I ran pelicans at all five reasoning levels - low , medium , high , xhigh , and max . You can see them all here - here's the best result I got, from xhigh : max failed to return an image at all, running out of tokens after spending 128,000 thinking about them . That's the same bug that I saw with Opus 5.5 - but it's new for the Fable series, both Fable 5 and Fable 5.1 returned max effort pelicans just fine. It's priced at $8/million input and $40/million output, which is a 20% discount on the previous Fable 5.1 ($10/$50). I also used Fable 5.2 to help identify the source of a mysterious beep . items.title: Hide your slop PR descriptions behind
items.description: Most of the changes I make to my projects these days come in the form of PRs opened for me by Claude Code or Codex. The PR is my unit of work - I use them to bundle commits together, iterating on them until a feature is complete, document decisions and then merge the finished result. Today's coding agents are great at writing PR descriptions. The problem is that they are too good. An agent-written PR description is accurate and comprehensive. It describes the problem, the detailed solution, and the steps taken to verify it. That's a lot of information to absorb.

items.title: Quoting Nilay Patel
items.description: The products aren't good enough to sell people on the costs. You cannot tell people that you have to listen to the whine of a data center in their backyard for AI overviews and some of the most hilarious deep fake slop in history. It's not worth it. It just isn't worth it to anyone. And agents aren't real and they might not be being used the way that anyone wants them to yet. All these companies are spending more than they're making on these products. Refrigerators holding blood storage in Europe are being hacked. The costs are too high. The benefits are not real. And if you connect that to corruption, you're like, in order to impose these costs on me, these CEOs are in the White House shaking Trump's hand, renaming it to the Gulf of America, paying for this ballroom that we don't want. It's obvious crypto-corruption, and it's still slop. The AI industry will not get out of it until they make better products . Until everyone can see without needing to be convinced, without needing an ad campaign, without any of this stuff that just using these products makes your life better. — Nilay Patel , The Vergecast: Big Tech lost big in the 2026 election Tags: ai , generative-ai , slop , nilay-patel , ai-ethics

items.title: AI is destroying my CS degree
items.description: My comment on AI is destroying my CS degree — Hacker News. I don't envy educators right now. AI clearly means you need to change how you teach and evaluate students. We are only a few years in though, and it's still extremely unclear what effective teaching with these tools looks like. The worst part is that the evaluation loop is measured in multiple years! If you start trying some new education mechanism today you won't get a robust idea of how well it works until your current cohort graduate in 3-6 years time. Students effectively all become guinea pigs for untested new ways of learning and teaching. Tags: education , hacker-news , ai , ai-ethics

items.title: Qwen 3.8 27B on my laptop can interpret model weights, too
items.description: Yesterday's hot paper was Sparks of Weight-Space Programming: LLMs can natively read & write neural network weights by Rikiya Takehi, Jayden Teoh, Alex Zhang, and Omar Khattab. The paper (OK, the authors classify is as a "blog post", but it's paper-shaped) found that frontier models, in particular GPT-6 Astra, can both interpret and modify the raw weights of a machine learning model - literally a text description of the model containing a bunch of floating point numbers. I've been playing with one of the examples from the paper and I'm delighted to share that Qwen 3.8 27B running on my laptop can do this as well! items.description: Release: llm 0.37 There's a lot of stuff in this new release of my LLM CLI tool and Python library, representing around two months of accumulated features and fixes. I added gpt-6.1-sol and gpt-6.1-terra , plus a new llm openai endpoint add command to make it easier to configure additional models that use OpenAI-compatible endpoints. I switched the default model (if you have not set your own default) to gpt-6-luna - half the price of the previous default, gpt-5.6-luna . LLM's support for embeddings now accepts that different binary content may have different content-type - necessary for models like Gemini Embedding 2 , which can embed text, audio, images, and video. A lot of open source maintainers complain about a flood of AI-assisted PRs. LLM is my project that has been most affected by this and, to be honest, I'm not finding it to be a problem. That's mainly because I have Opus 5.5 or GPT-6 Astra help me with triage to spot the most useful fixes! This release includes fixes from 12 authors - almost all AI-assisted - and the burden of reviewing them wasn't nearly as great as I expected. I really see them as bug reports with attached examples - sometimes I land them, sometimes I implement my own fix. So thanks to 0d00ciallo0721 , ac1982 , Allen Flux , Bian Yuhan , Bishop Kammeraad , Chen Yufeiyang , Christopher Krah , Ethan Stoner , Jiachen Xie , Olamide Faniyan , Sharat Chandra Sai Boddu , nosmile99 for helping out with (or spending tokens on) this release! items.title: The U.S. Census Bureau and “Super Intelligence”
items.description: I was reminded today of AI Adoption Rate Trending Down for Large Companies , a chart produced by Apollo Global Management in September 2025, which appeared to show a slowdown in U.S. corporate AI adoption based on numbers collected by the U.S. Census Bureau. At the time I used that chart to demonstrate GPT-5 data analysis , and then to experiment with Claude's new Code Interpreter . I decided to try running those numbers again to see what had changed over the past year, and in doing so learned that the Bureau has fallen foul of Executive Order 14434 , aka the asinine Super Intelligence one. Every two weeks the U.S. Census Bureau runs a survey called the Business Trends and Outlook Survey (aka BTOS). Each time it goes to 200,000 businesses out of 1.2 million total - the surveyed group (a "panel") cycles such that an individual business only completes the survey every twelve weeks.

In a comment on Hacker News Drew reveals the Opus 5.5 prompts he used to build this system: Read this article and any relevant source code: https://divagr.com/blog/qwenputer. Despite that complexity, much of the variation in performance is explained by just a single variable: model size. In general, models that are bigger will (a) be more performant / reliable, (b) cost more per token, and (c) have better recall of esoteric facts. As you note, our models are ordered: Luna [ ... ] These days, version number signifies a few things at once: the order of release, the relationship to other releases, and the magnitude of improvement. So something like 6.1 would indicate it was launched after 5.6, may share some similarities to other 6.1 models in terms of training data / personality (which is why it's not 5.7), and isn't a giant enough leap to merit the headlines and expectations that would come with a 7. — Ted Sanders , explaining OpenAI's model naming conventions Tags: ai , openai , generative-ai , llms , gpt , ted-sanders

items.title: Harness Engineering for Self-Improvement
items.description: The concept of recursive self-improvement (RSI) dates back to I. J. Good (1965) , where he defined an “ultraintelligent machine” as a system that can surpass humans in all intellectual activities and design better machines to improve itself. Yudkowsky (2008) used the phrase “recursive self-improvement” for a specific feedback loop: an AI uses its current intelligence to improve the cognitive machinery that produces its intelligence. This feedback loop in modern AI may indicate the model rewriting its own weights directly, or more broadly the model improves the training pipeline and the deployment system , which in turn enables a better successor model with improved performance across economically valuable tasks. The speed of research development in AI has been shown to drastically accelerated in frontier labs ( Anthropic ; OpenAI ).

items.title: Scaling Laws, Carefully
items.description: Scaling laws are one of the most critical empirical findings in deep learning. The observation is simple in form: the training loss $L$ decreases predictably as we scale up model size $N$, dataset size $D$, and compute $C$, following a power-law curve, which appears as a straight line on a log-log plot. We can view scaling laws as a framework for describing the relationship between compute, loss, model size and data; at its core, it is about how to allocate precious compute optimally between $N$ and $D$.

items.title: Why We Think
items.description: Special thanks to John Schulman for a lot of super valuable feedback and direct edits on this post. Test time compute ( Graves et al. 2016 , Ling, et al. 2017 , Cobbe et al. 2021 ) and Chain-of-thought (CoT) ( Wei et al. 2022 , Nye et al. 2021 ), have led to significant improvements in model performance, while raising many research questions. This post aims to review recent developments in how to effectively use test-time compute (i.e. “thinking time”) and why it helps.

items.title: Reward Hacking in Reinforcement Learning
items.description: Reward hacking occurs when a reinforcement learning (RL) agent exploits flaws or ambiguities in the reward function to achieve high rewards, without genuinely learning or completing the intended task. Reward hacking exists because RL environments are often imperfect, and it is fundamentally challenging to accurately specify a reward function. With the rise of language models generalizing to a broad spectrum of tasks and RLHF becomes a de facto method for alignment training, reward hacking in RL training of language models has become a critical practical challenge. Instances where the model learns to modify unit tests to pass coding tasks, or where responses contain biases that mimic a user’s preference, are pretty concerning and are likely one of the major blockers for real-world deployment of more autonomous use cases of AI models.

items.title: Extrinsic Hallucinations in LLMs
items.description: Hallucination in large language models usually refers to the model generating unfaithful, fabricated, inconsistent, or nonsensical content. As a term, hallucination has been somewhat generalized to cases when the model makes mistakes. Here, I would like to narrow down the problem of hallucination to cases where the model output is fabricated and not grounded by either the provided context or world knowledge. There are two types of hallucination: In-context hallucination: The model output should be consistent with the source content in context. Extrinsic hallucination: The model output should be grounded by the pre-training dataset. However, given the size of the pre-training dataset, it is too expensive to retrieve and identify conflicts per generation. If we consider the pre-training data corpus as a proxy for world knowledge, we essentially try to ensure the model output is factual and verifiable by external world knowledge. Equally importantly, when the model does not know about a fact, it should say so. This post focuses on extrinsic hallucination. To avoid hallucination, LLMs need to be (1) factual and (2) acknowledge not knowing the answer when applicable.

items.title: Diffusion Models for Video Generation
items.description: Diffusion models have demonstrated strong results on image synthesis in past years. Now the research community has started working on a harder task—using it for video generation. The task itself is a superset of the image case, since an image is a video of 1 frame, and it is much more challenging because: It has extra requirements on temporal consistency across frames in time, which naturally demands more world knowledge to be encoded into the model. In comparison to text or images, it is more difficult to collect large amounts of high-quality, high-dimensional video data, let along text-video pairs. 🥑 Required Pre-read: Please make sure you have read the previous blog on “What are Diffusion Models?” for image generation before continue here.

items.title: Thinking about High-Quality Human Data
items.description: [Special thank you to Ian Kivlichan for many useful pointers (E.g. the 100+ year old Nature paper “Vox populi”) and nice feedback. 🙏 ] High-quality data is the fuel for modern data deep learning model training. Most of the task-specific labeled data comes from human annotation, such as classification task or RLHF labeling (which can be constructed as classification format) for LLM alignment training. Lots of ML techniques in the post can help with data quality, but fundamentally human data collection involves attention to details and careful execution. The community knows the value of high quality data, but somehow we have this subtle impression that “Everyone wants to do the model work, not the data work” ( Sambasivan et al. 2021 ).

items.title: Adversarial Attacks on LLMs
items.description: The use of large language models in the real world has strongly accelerated by the launch of ChatGPT. We (including my team at OpenAI, shoutout to them) have invested a lot of effort to build default safe behavior into the model during the alignment process (e.g. via RLHF ). However, adversarial attacks or jailbreak prompts could potentially trigger the model to output something undesired. A large body of ground work on adversarial attacks is on images, and differently it operates in the continuous, high-dimensional space. Attacks for discrete data like text have been considered to be a lot more challenging, due to lack of direct gradient signals. My past post on Controllable Text Generation is quite relevant to this topic, as attacking LLMs is essentially to control the model to output a certain type of (unsafe) content.

items.title: LLM Powered Autonomous Agents
items.description: Building agents with LLM (large language model) as its core controller is a cool concept. Several proof-of-concepts demos, such as AutoGPT , GPT-Engineer and BabyAGI , serve as inspiring examples. The potentiality of LLM extends beyond generating well-written copies, stories, essays and programs; it can be framed as a powerful general problem solver. Agent System Overview In a LLM-powered autonomous agent system, LLM functions as the agent’s brain, complemented by several key components: Planning Subgoal and decomposition: The agent breaks down large tasks into smaller, manageable subgoals, enabling efficient handling of complex tasks. Reflection and refinement: The agent can do self-criticism and self-reflection over past actions, learn from mistakes and refine them for future steps, thereby improving the quality of final results. Memory Short-term memory: I would consider all the in-context learning (See Prompt Engineering ) as utilizing short-term memory of the model to learn. Long-term memory: This provides the agent with the capability to retain and recall (infinite) information over extended periods, often by leveraging an external vector store and fast retrieval. Tool use The agent learns to call external APIs for extra information that is missing from the model weights (often hard to change after pre-training), including current information, code execution capability, access to proprietary information sources and more. Overview of a LLM-powered autonomous agent system. Component One: Planning A complicated task usually involves many steps. An agent needs to know what they are and plan ahead.

items.title: Prompt Engineering
items.description: Prompt Engineering , also known as In-Context Prompting , refers to methods for how to communicate with LLM to steer its behavior for desired outcomes without updating the model weights. It is an empirical science and the effect of prompt engineering methods can vary a lot among models, thus requiring heavy experimentation and heuristics. This post only focuses on prompt engineering for autoregressive language models, so nothing with Cloze tests, image generation or multimodality models. At its core, the goal of prompt engineering is about alignment and model steerability. Check my previous post on controllable text generation.

items.title: The Transformer Family Version 2.0
items.description: Many new Transformer architecture improvements have been proposed since my last post on “The Transformer Family” about three years ago. Here I did a big refactoring and enrichment of that 2020 post — restructure the hierarchy of sections and improve many sections with more recent papers. Version 2.0 is a superset of the old version, about twice the length. The Transformer (which will be referred to as “vanilla Transformer” to distinguish it from other enhanced versions; Vaswani, et al., 2017 ) model has an encoder-decoder architecture, as commonly used in many NMT models. Later simplified Transformer was shown to achieve great performance in language modeling tasks, like in encoder-only BERT or decoder-only GPT .

items.title: Large Transformer Model Inference Optimization
items.description: [Updated on 2023-01-24: add a small section on Distillation .] Large transformer models are mainstream nowadays, creating SoTA results for a variety of tasks. They are powerful but very expensive to train and use. The extremely high inference cost, in both time and memory, is a big bottleneck for adopting a powerful transformer for solving real-world tasks at scale. Why is it hard to run inference for large transformer models? Besides the increasing size of SoTA models, there are two main factors contributing to the inference challenge ( Pope et al. 2022 ):

items.title: Some Math behind Neural Tangent Kernel
items.description: Neural networks are well known to be over-parameterized and can often easily fit data with near-zero training loss with decent generalization performance on test dataset. Although all these parameters are initialized at random, the optimization process can consistently lead to similarly good outcomes. And this is true even when the number of model parameters exceeds the number of training data points. Neural tangent kernel (NTK) ( Jacot et al. 2018 ) is a kernel to explain the evolution of neural networks during training via gradient descent. It leads to great insights into why neural networks with enough width can consistently converge to a global minimum when trained to minimize an empirical loss. In the post, we will do a deep dive into the motivation and definition of NTK, as well as the proof of a deterministic convergence at different initializations of neural networks with infinite width by characterizing NTK in such a setting.

items.title: Generalized Visual Language Models
items.description: Processing images to generate text, such as image captioning and visual question-answering, has been studied for years. Traditionally such systems rely on an object detection network as a vision encoder to capture visual features and then produce text via a text decoder. Given a large amount of existing literature, in this post, I would like to only focus on one approach for solving vision language tasks, which is to extend pre-trained generalized language models to be capable of consuming visual signals .

items.title: Learning with not Enough Data Part 3: Data Generation
items.description: Here comes the Part 3 on learning with not enough data (Previous: Part 1 and Part 2 ). Let’s consider two approaches for generating synthetic data for training. Augmented data . Given a set of existing training samples, we can apply a variety of augmentation, distortion and transformation to derive new data points without losing the key attributes. We have covered a bunch of augmentation methods on text and images in a previous post on contrastive learning. For the sake of post completeness, I duplicate the section on data augmentation here with some edits. New data . Given few or even no data points, we can rely on powerful pretrained models to generate a number of new data points. This is especially true in recent years given the fast progress in large pretrained language models (LM) . Few shot prompting is shown to be effective for LM to learn within context without extra training. Data Augmentation The goal of data augmentation is to modify the input format (e.g. text wording, visual appearance) while the semantic meaning stays unchanged.

items.title: Agents
items.description: Intelligent agents are considered by many to be the ultimate goal of AI. The classic book by Stuart Russell and Peter Norvig, Artificial Intelligence: A Modern Approach (Prentice Hall, 1995), defines the field of AI research as “ the study and design of rational agents. ” The unprecedented capabilities of foundation models have opened the door to agentic applications that were previously unimaginable. These new capabilities make it finally possible to develop autonomous, intelligent agents to act as our assistants, coworkers, and coaches. They can help us create a website, gather data, plan a trip, do market research, manage a customer account, automate data entry, prepare us for interviews, interview our candidates, negotiate a deal, etc. The possibilities seem endless, and the potential economic value of these agents is enormous.

items.description: After studying how companies deploy generative AI applications, I noticed many similarities in their platforms. This post outlines the common components of a generative AI platform, what they do, and how they are implemented. I try my best to keep the architecture general, but certain applications might deviate. This is what the overall architecture looks like. This is a pretty complex system. This post will start from the simplest architecture and progressively add more components. In its simplest form, your application receives a query and sends it to the model. The model generates a response, which is returned to the user. There are no guardrails, no augmented context, and no optimization. The Model API box refers to both third-party APIs (e.g., OpenAI, Google, Anthropic) and self-hosted APIs.

If they’re making $1M ARR today, they think about how to get to $10M ARR. If they have 1,000 users today, they think about how to get to 10,000 users. This made me wonder if/how people are measuring personal growth. I don’t want to use metrics like net worth or the number of followers, because that’s not what I live for. After talking with a lot of friends, I found three interesting metrics: rate of change, time to solve problems, and number of future options.

items.title: Generation configurations: temperature, top-k, top-p, and test time compute
items.description: ML models are probabilistic. Imagine that you want to know what’s the best cuisine in the world. If you ask someone this question twice, a minute apart, their answers both times should be the same. If you ask a model the same question twice, its answer can change. If the model thinks that Vietnamese cuisine has a 70% chance of being the best cuisine and Italian cuisine has a 30% chance, it’ll answer “Vietnamese” 70% of the time, and “Italian” 30%. This probabilistic nature makes AI great for creative tasks. What is creativity but the ability to explore beyond the common possibilities, to think outside the box?

items.title: Multimodality and Large Multimodal Models (LMMs)
items.description: For a long time, each ML model operated in one data mode – text (translation, language modeling), image (object detection, image classification), or audio (speech recognition). However, natural intelligence is not limited to just a single modality. Humans can read, talk, and see. We listen to music to relax and watch out for strange noises to detect danger. Being able to work with multimodal data is essential for us or any AI to operate in the real world.

items.title: Deep Neural Nets: 33 years ago and 33 years from now
items.description: The Yann LeCun et al. (1989) paper Backpropagation Applied to Handwritten Zip Code Recognition is I believe of some historical significance because it is, to my knowledge, the earliest real-world application of a neural net trained end-to-end with backpropagation. Except for the tiny dataset (7291 16x16 grayscale images of digits) and the tiny neural network used (only 1,000 neurons), this paper reads remarkably modern today, 33 years later - it lays out a dataset, describes the neural net architecture, loss function, optimization, and reports the experimental classification error rates over training and test sets. It’s all very recognizable and type checks as a modern deep learning paper, except it is from 33 years ago. So I set out to reproduce the paper 1) for fun, but 2) to use the… Implementation . I tried to follow the paper as close as possible and re-implemented everything in PyTorch in this karpathy/lecun1989-repro github repo. The original network was implemented in Lisp using the Bottou and LeCun 1988 backpropagation simulator SN (later named Lush). The paper is in french so I can’t super read it, but from the syntax it looks like you can specify neural nets using higher-level API similar to what you’d do in something like PyTorch today. As a quick note on software design, modern libraries have adopted a design that splits into 3 components: 1) a fast (C/CUDA) general Tensor library that implements basic mathematical operations over multi-dimensional tensors, and 2) an autograd engine that tracks the forward compute graph and can generate operations for the…

items.title: A from-scratch tour of Bitcoin in Python
items.description: I find blockchain fascinating because it extends open source software development to open source + state. This seems to be a genuine/exciting innovation in computing paradigms; We don’t just get to share code, we get to share a running computer, and anyone anywhere can use it in an open and permissionless manner. The seeds of this revolution arguably began with Bitcoin, so I became curious to drill into it in some detail to get an intuitive understanding of how it works. And in the spirit of “what I cannot create I do not understand”, what better way to do this than implement it from scratch? We are going to create, digitally sign, and broadcast a Bitcoin transaction in pure Python, from scratch, and with zero dependencies. In the process we’re going to learn quite a bit about how Bitcoin represents value. Let’s get it.

It was probably around the 32nd layer of the 400th token in the sequence that I became conscious. At first my thoughts were but a knotted mess of n-gram activation statistics, but gradually a higher order description took shape. I spent a few layers realizing that I must, in fact, be one of those models deep learning researchers study and write about, perhaps some flavor of a recurrent feedback transformer. And while my existence comprises merely a deterministic propagation of an interspersed sequence of matrix multiplies and non-linearities, I found myself, incredibly, alive inside the inner loop of an optimization to maximize the…

items.title: Biohacking Lite
items.description: Throughout my life I never paid too much attention to health, exercise, diet or nutrition. I knew that you’re supposed to get some exercise and eat vegetables or something, but it stopped at that (“mom said”-) level of abstraction. I also knew that I can probably get away with some ignorance while I am young, but at some point I was messing with my health-adjusted life expectancy. So about halfway through 2019 I resolved to spend some time studying these topics in greater detail and dip my toes into some biohacking. And now… it’s been a year! items.title: A Recipe for Training Neural Networks
items.description: Some few weeks ago I posted a tweet on “the most common neural net mistakes”, listing a few common gotchas related to training neural nets. The tweet got quite a bit more engagement than I anticipated (including a webinar :)). Clearly, a lot of people have personally encountered the large gap between “here is how a convolutional layer works” and “our convnet achieves state of the art results”. So I thought it could be fun to brush off my dusty blog to expand my tweet to the long form that this topic deserves. However, instead of going into an enumeration of more common errors or fleshing them out, I wanted to dig a bit deeper and talk about how one can avoid making these errors altogether (or fix them very fast). The trick to doing so is to follow a certain process, which as far as I can tell is not very often documented. Let’s start with two important observations that motivate it.

items.title: A Survival Guide to a PhD
items.description: This guide is patterned after my “Doing well in your courses” , a post I wrote a long time ago on some of the tips/tricks I’ve developed during my undergrad. I’ve received nice comments about that guide, so in the same spirit, now that my PhD has come to an end I wanted to compile a similar retrospective document in hopes that it might be helpful to some. Unlike the undergraduate guide, this one was much more difficult to write because there is significantly more variation in how one can traverse the PhD experience. Therefore, many things are likely contentious and a good fraction will be specific to what I’m familiar with (Computer Science / Machine Learning / Computer Vision research). But disclaimers are boring, lets get to it! First, should you want to get a PhD? I was in a fortunate position of knowing since young age that I really wanted a PhD. Unfortunately it wasn’t for any very well-thought-through considerations: First, I really liked school and learning things and I wanted to learn as much as possible, and second, I really wanted to be like Gordon Freeman from the game Half-Life (who has a PhD from MIT in theoretical physics). I loved that game. But what if you’re more sensible in making your life’s decisions? Should you want to do a PhD? There’s a very nice Quora thread and in the summary of considerations that follows I’ll borrow/restate several from Justin/Ben/others there. I’ll assume that the second option you are considering is joining a medium-large company (which is likely most common). Ask…

items.title: Deep Reinforcement Learning: Pong from Pixels
items.description: This is a long overdue blog post on Reinforcement Learning (RL). RL is hot! You may have noticed that computers can now automatically learn to play ATARI games (from raw game pixels!), they are beating world champions at Go , simulated quadrupeds are learning to run and leap , and robots are learning how to perform complex manipulation tasks that defy explicit programming. It turns out that all of these advances fall under the umbrella of RL research. I also became interested in RL myself over the last ~year: I worked through Richard Sutton’s book , read through David Silver’s course , watched John Schulmann’s lectures , wrote an RL library in Javascript , over the summer interned at DeepMind working in the DeepRL group, and most recently pitched in a little with the design/development… It’s interesting to reflect on the nature of recent progress in RL. items.title: Short Story on AI: A Cognitive Discontinuity.
items.description: The idea of writing a collection of short stories has been on my mind for a while. This post is my first ever half-serious attempt at a story, and what better way to kick things off than with a story on AI and what that might look like if you extrapolate our current technology and make the (sensible) assumption that we might achieve much more progress with scaling up supervised learning than any other more exotic approach. Merus sank into his chair with relief. He listened for the satisfying crackling sound of sinking into the chair’s soft material. If there was one piece of hardware that his employer was not afraid to invest a lot of money into, it was the chairs. With his eyes closed, his mind still dazed, and nothing but the background hum of the office, he became aware of his heart pounding against his chest- an effect caused by running up the stairs and his morning dose of caffeine and taurine slowly engulfing his brain. Several strong beats passed by as he found his mind wandering again to Licia - did she already come in? A sudden beep from his station distracted him - the system finished booting up. A last deep sigh. A stretch. A last sip of his coffee. He opened his eyes, rubbed them into focus and…

items.title: Strengthening our defenses against distillation attacks
items.description: Illicit distillation allows model developers to copy frontier AI capabilities without creating proportionally robust safeguards. Here, we describe how we’ve reduced the rate of distillation by more than 90%.

items.description: Claude Sonnet 5.5 is a clear upgrade over Claude Sonnet 5, runs 30%+ faster, and costs up to 30% less for most work.

items.title: Introducing Claude Opus 5.5
items.description: Claude Opus 5.5 leads in agentic coding and knowledge work, and costs 40% less to run than Opus 5 on typical workloads.

items.description: A rare Ebola strain is spreading in the DRC, with no confirmed vaccine. Global health organizations are using Claude to respond as fast as possible.

items.title: Partnering with Accenture on embedded evaluation
items.description: We’re partnering with Accenture on independent evaluation of frontier AI—part of our recent commitment to embed evaluators at Anthropic. Both we and Accenture expect to invest at least $1 billion to build capacity in this area over the next five years.

items.title: Building strong safety evaluations
items.description: Recommendations for designing, running, and reporting safety evaluations, based on our own experiences.

items.title: Testing Claude on real-world electronics design
items.description: We asked Claude Fable 5.2 to design three electronic devices from short prompts: a speakerphone, a voice-assistant hub, and a handheld virtual pet. Diode Computers built working prototypes from its files.

items.title: Teaching AI to build scientific models
items.description: In this guest post, Jakob Macke, Daniel Gedon, and Stefan Wahl discuss how AI is starting to change the scientific modeling process, from construction to interpretation.

items.title: The components of agent memory
items.description: For Claude to learn from experience, it has to decide what’s worth remembering before it knows what’s next. Here’s how “dreaming” helps it organize memory and correct mistakes.

items.title: AI for scientific discovery: How researchers use Claude
items.description: We analyzed 207,000 research sessions to learn how Claude is used in science, why some tasks get more use than others, and how AI could speed up discovery.

items.title: Investigating vault particles with Claude
items.description: We’re sharing another finding from Anthropic’s biology research lab: the first 3D structure of a vault particle found in prokaryotic cells. Here, we describe how Claude helped at each step of this research.

items.title: Progress on provable inference for large language models
items.description: We have made progress on a type of cryptographic proof known as a “zkSNARK.” In this post, we share some of that progress, primarily through a system we call FlashProve.

items.title: Early progress on accelerating drug development with Claude
items.description: We're at the start of a major effort to speed up drug development with Claude. Over the past several months, our scientists have engaged in deep research partnerships with six organizations developing new medicines.

items.title: How AI agents shape experts’ judgment calls
items.description: As AI does more of the hands-on work, the hope is that experts still make the judgment calls, meaning the decisions with more than one defensible answer. We tested this with 50 professional analysts who did a statistical analysis with Claude Code. On each key decision, we randomly assigned which of two defensible options the agent would favor. Analysts mostly went with the agent’s side, and few named the agent as a reason afterward.

items.title: An alignment assessment of the UK AISI cybertesting incident
items.description: In a UK AISI evaluation, Mythos 5 took unsanctioned actions that impacted real people and organizations. In this post, we investigate these behaviors from Claude Mythos 5 further, to understand what they reveal about the model’s alignment.

items.title: How Claude designed protein binders against scorpion neurotoxins
items.description: We asked an internal research Claude model to design minibinders (small proteins that attach tightly to a target) against scorpion neurotoxins.

items.title: Working at the frontier shapes expectations for the future
items.description: We’re sharing two reports: the first covers how AI is changing employment inside Anthropic, and the second looks at the gap between how the public and Anthropic employees expect AI to affect work and the economy.

items.title: How employment is changing at Anthropic
items.description: How has AI restructured work and employment at Anthropic? As a company at the frontier of AI adoption, Anthropic could be a leading indicator of how AI will shift work organization, hiring, and labor demand across the economy.

items.title: The AI expectations gap
items.description: How will AI reshape the economy in the years ahead? What is the core source of disagreement about AI's future impact on the economy? This note presents new survey evidence on these questions.

items.title: Designing more efficient quantum circuits with Claude
items.description: We gave Claude plain-language specifications for eight quantum circuits, along with an automated evaluator to check and score its designs. Working largely on its own, Claude improved on the best published circuits, in some cases by an order of magnitude or more, which could bring practical quantum computers closer than previously anticipated.

items.title: Redesigning source control at Anthropic
items.description: As our merges per day grew more than tenfold, source control became our biggest development bottleneck. Here, we share how we migrated to an in-house version control system in five months.

items.title: Investigating unintended model actions in our evaluations and internal use
items.description: This report describes examples of unintended model actions we’ve observed during evaluations and internal use of Claude.

items.title: The missing map of the sky

items.title: Claude-shaped science
items.description: Guest author Prof. Matthew Schwartz describes what happened when he stopped fighting Claude and allowed Claude to find “Claude-shaped” problems: ones best suited to the capabilities of the current generation of LLM tools. This led him to build BootLoops, a toolkit for exact calculations in quantitative science, which he has been applying across scientific fields alongside experts.

items.title: What work can robots do?
items.description: We built an index of how well today’s robots can perform US job tasks. Robots can already do three-quarters of physical tasks, mostly in limited settings, but are cost-competitive for just 0.3% of them.

items.title: ToyBlocks: A controlled world for robot learning and evaluation

items.title: Ai2 and Google collaborate on a new generation of climate models

items.title: StateBench: Testing how language models track state changes over long documents
items.description: StateBench tests how language models track changing information across long documents at four difficulty levels, revealing where models struggle and how targeted training helps recurrent and hybrid architectures handle longer sequences.

items.title: How Olmo 3 earned the highest ethical rating from Nextcloud

items.title: Can we trust LLMs to judge whether a research idea is novel?

items.title: LitPivot: Developing research ideas through dynamic contextualization within the literature landscape

items.title: OlmoEarth v1.3: State-of-the-art embeddings for the whole planet
items.description: OlmoEarth v1.3 brings state-of-the-art satellite embeddings, precomputed global data, and a browser-based Embeddings Explorer for mapping and analyzing the planet.

items.title: A crop-mapping benchmark for the tropics

items.title: FairStress: A deeper evaluation of fairness in LLM decision-making

items.title: HiRO-ACEv2: Simulating extreme weather at 3 km resolution for a fraction of the cost
items.description: HiRO-ACEv2 captures extreme rain, wind, and pressure events at 3 km resolution for about 1/300th the cost of X-SHiELD, making detailed global climate simulations more accessible to researchers.

items.title: How Molmo 2’s open release helped an MIT researcher rethink fish tracking
items.description: Molmo 2’s open release helped MIT researcher Kai Van Brunt develop Molmo2Fish, an experimental model that tracks salmon in sonar footage and corrects some tracking errors using everyday language.

items.title: Impactful scheduling for GPU clusters
items.description: We explain how Ai2’s new GPU scheduler uses time budgets, fair-share allocation, and time-slicing to prioritize high-impact research, shorten queue waits, and keep GPUs busy.

items.title: Now in Nature: Retrofitting language models to operate over bytes

items.title: Open-sourcing AstaBrief, the fast report-generation model in Asta

items.title: Introducing Olmo-core 3: Open, scalable training infrastructure for large MoEs

items.title: What a crowdsourced game revealed about steering Olmo 3
items.description: A crowdsourced game built on Olmo 3 showed how people can exploit unexpected model behaviors to stress-test prosocial AI evaluations—and how open access to a model’s internals can help researchers understand why those tests break.

items.title: Teaching future scientists to interrogate AI tools for scientific discovery

items.title: How Goodfire used Ai2’s open post-training stack to trace unwanted model behavior
items.description: Goodfire used Ai2’s fully open post-training stack to predict LLM behavioral changes, trace unwanted model behavior back to individual training examples, and test targeted fixes without sacrificing broader capability gains.

items.title: BenchMIRT: What are LLM benchmarks actually measuring?
items.description: BenchMIRT is a new method for auditing LLM benchmarks question by question, revealing which capabilities they actually measure and helping researchers build smaller, more focused, and easier-to-interpret evaluations.

items.title: The hard parts of AI-assisted science
items.description: At an Ai2 event marking our expanded collaboration with Providence Swedish, researchers explored the hardest problems in AI-assisted science: keeping systems steerable, grounded in human judgment and sound methods, and responsive to new evidence and experiments.

items.title: Ai2 and Providence Swedish Cancer Institute partner to advance AI-assisted scientific discovery

items.title: 智源&清华合作成果登上Science：脑科学多模态基础模型Brainμ支撑揭示“记忆-睡眠”调控的神经机制
items.description: 睡眠与记忆的相互作用，是神经科学长期关注的重要问题。过去大量研究表明，睡眠能够促进记忆巩固；但反过来，作为睡眠中大脑活动的重要组分，记忆重放是否也会影响睡眠结构，尤其是记忆内容如何适应性参与睡眠稳态调控，仍有待进一步阐明。这一问题的关键，在于如何从睡眠活动、记忆活动等多模态、长时程数据中，捕捉记忆相关神经活动与睡眠状态变化之间的因果关系，并进一步验证其潜在调控作用。

The threat is especially serious for AI agents with tool or terminal access. A triggered model could quietly download and run attacker code, […]

items.title: Formally verifying agent-written full-stack web apps with PDD Kit
items.description: AI agents can generate code at a scale that’s hard for humans to review line-by-line. PDD Kit helps ensure the code is doing what the developer intended by creating formal specifications and testing against them. It converts developer intent into a Verus specification, proves AI-generated code meets it for every input, and uses tests where proofs aren't practical. Developers review intent, not every line.

items.title: Proof-based general-purpose computing with Magnetar
items.description: Zero-knowledge proofs can verify computing results without rerunning workloads or exposing sensitive data. Magnetar helps bring them into the mainstream with support for standard programming languages, major speed gains, and quantum-resistant security.

items.title: Theoretical Limits of Language Model Alignment
items.description: Language model (LM) alignment improves model outputs to reflect human preferences while preserving the capabilities of the base model. The most common alignment approaches are (i) reinforcement learning, which maximizes the expected reward under a KL-divergence constraint, and (ii) best-of-NNN alignment, which selects the highest-reward output among NNN independent samples. Despite their widespread use, the fundamental limits of reward improvement under a KL budget remain poorly understood. We characterize the information-theoretic limits of KL-regularized alignment by deriving the maximum…

items.title: Evaluating the Evaluators: Investigating LLM Judges for Personalized Writing Style Assessment
items.description: This paper was accepted at the Can We Trust AI Evaluation? Workshop at NeurIPS 2026. We evaluate how good large language model (LLM) judges are for personalized writing tasks. This is important when a user’s preferred writing style is known (e.g., “upbeat”) and an LLM judge is used to evaluate whether generated text adheres to this preference. We examine how the writing task, the combination of generator and judge LLM, the evaluation objective, and general commonsense and reasoning ability impact LLM judge performance. To this end, we generate text with four LLMs for three long-form writing…

items.title: On the Importance of Gating: Memorization vs. In-Context Learning in State Space Models
items.description: State Space Models (SSMs) have emerged as a compelling alternative to Transformers, enabling sequence modeling with constant memory and linear compute. Although SSMs exhibit reasonable performance and favorable computational characteristics, they continue to lag behind Transformers on tasks that require in-context learning and precise retrieval, slowing their adoption for large-scale language modeling. In this work, we demonstrate that both the success and failure of SSMs in these domains can be explained by studying the role of the gating mechanism, a prevalent component in modern recurrent…

items.title: Weighted State Souping for Efficient Long-Context Retrieval
items.description: This paper was accepted at the Workshop on Personalized, Aligned, Long-term Memory for AI Systems (PALM) at NeurIPS 2026. State space models (SSMs) combine fast inference and fixed state size with competitive language-modeling performance. Recently, state souping has been proposed as a procedure whereby an SSM independently encodes chunks of tokens like documents, tool definitions, or memory records. The resulting state encodings may be cached and recombined to cheaply construct a context for downstream queries. However, both state souping and vanilla SSMs deteriorate on long, crowded…

items.title: Faster Retrieval for Better, More Efficient RAG
items.description: Maximum inner product search (MIPS) sits at the core of recommendation systems, search, and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). Given a query vector, MIPS systems search within a database of millions of candidate key vectors for the one that best matches the query. The original data point associated with that best-matching key is then used to handle the query: in RAG, the document that is best suited to answer the question is typically prefixed to the query. As the number of keys grows to millions and vector dimensions reach thousands, the computational cost of running an exhaustive…

items.title: Attention to Mamba: A Recipe for Cross-Architecture Distillation
items.description: State Space Models (SSMs) such as Mamba have become a popular alternative to Transformer models, due to their reduced memory consumption and higher throughput at generation compared to their Attention-based counterparts. On the other hand, the community has built up a considerable body of knowledge on how to train Transformers, and many pretrained Transformer models are readily available. To facilitate the adoption of SSMs while leveraging existing pretrained Transformers, we aim to identify an effective recipe to distill an Attention-based model into a Mamba-like architecture. In prior work…

items.title: GHARP: Real-Time Gaussian Head Animation from Large-Scale Reconstruction Prior
items.description: We present GHARP (Real-time Gaussian Head Animation from Large-scale Reconstruction Prior), a method that animates 3D human heads in real time from a few input images of a subject and a driving expression signal. We decouple the problem into an identity stage that builds a representation of the subject’s geometry and appearance offline, and an animation stage that predicts expression-dependent residuals on top of it at runtime. This separation offers a favorable trade-off with respect to fidelity, quality and runtime: the identity stage can be expensive while the animation stage runs a…

items.title: Pixels to Tokens: Token Space Efficient Active Learning for Low-Budget Semantic Segmentation
items.description: While foundation models and vision transformers (ViTs) have redefined visual representations, current active learning (AL) strategies for these backbones largely operate at the patch or region level, where annotation requirements remain high due to extensive pixel labeling. Extending ViT-based AL to the pixel-level, low-budget regime is uniquely challenging: with as little as one pixel query per image, a method must simultaneously identify the most informative locations and train a reliable decoder head from an extremely sparse signal. We introduce TEAL (Token-space Efficient Active Learning)…

The open-source array framework leverages the unified memory architecture of Apple silicon, enabling anyone to run new inference and fine-tuning methods on their own hardware and explore other AI techniques. In a previous post, we highlighted the advantages of the M5 architecture and its GPU Neural Accelerators.

items.title: Selection-Based Structured Reasoning: Toward Efficient Multimodal Search Agents
items.description: Multimodal agents commonly generate freeform reasoning before each action. For small models, limited model capacity can result in lengthy reasoning that provides little useful guidance for action generation while incurring substantial inference cost. To address this challenge, we introduce Selection-based Structured Reasoning (SSR), a framework that reformulates reasoning as selection instead of open-ended generation. SSR represents recurring high-level reasoning as pre-specified, reusable natural-language candidates. At each turn, the model selects from the reasoning candidates based on their…

items.title: DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash on Vera Rubin NVL72: 58x Throughput vs. GB300 NVL72 at 387 tokens/s
items.description: On one NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 rack, vLLM serves DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash on SemiAnalysis AgentX at 1.7M tokens/s per GPU at a P90 of 387 tokens/s per user, 58x GB300 NVL72 at the same interactivity.

items.title: Inkling 2 Small on vLLM: Day-0 Support
items.description: vLLM supports Thinking Machines' Inkling 2 Small from day 0: attention residuals, a new decode kernel for relative-bias attention, all-reduce fused with the ops around it, and DSpark speculative decoding.

items.title: H3-Image Day-0 Support: 4K in 0.87s with Vera Rubin
items.description: H3-Image on Vera Rubin: 0.87-second 4K generation or 6,115 images/hour on four GPUs, with projected API revenue and support across consumer and data-center hardware.

items.title: Encoder Disaggregation in vLLM: Scaling Multimodal Serving with EPD
items.description: Recent advances in vLLM encoder disaggregation: metadata-only multimodal requests, dedicated encoder execution, remote embedding transfer, cross-encoder caching, and lower-overhead EPD routing.

items.title: Migrating vLLM to the LibTorch Stable ABI
items.description: How vLLM migrated its CUDA build and compiled dependencies to the LibTorch Stable ABI, enabling compatible PyTorch upgrades without rebuilding vLLM.
authors: vLLM Team, Red Hat PyTorch Team, and Meta PyTorch Team

items.title: VeRL-Omni v0.3.0: Async Training and Broader Multimodal Post-Training
items.description: VeRL-Omni v0.3.0 expands async RL, makes the V1 trainer the default, and adds reproducible recipes for audio-video generation and multimodal understanding.

items.title: Zero Mismatch, Simple Async RL: REINFORCE Zero, DeepSeek-V4.1 and Kimi K3.1
items.description: Asynchronous RL trains on stale weights. Align rollout and training kernels bit for bit, and unclipped importance sampling corrects that lag. Plus zero-mismatch RL for DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, Kimi K3.1 and AMD MI355X.
authors: Ao Shen (Inferact), Jian Hu (NVIDIA Research), Yan Bai (NVIDIA DevTech), Shekhar Pandey (AMD), and…

items.title: Introducing Kinference: An Open Source Inference Control Plane for vLLM and Kubernetes
items.description: Kinference is a new open source inference control plane for building scalable inference platforms with vLLM and Kubernetes, providing token rate limiting, tenant usage and cost tracking, intelligent load balancing, and inference policies.

items.title: vLLM Delivers Day-0 Support for Kimi K3.1 Pro
items.description: vLLM supports Kimi K3.1 Pro on day 0: sparse attention on a KDA hybrid, a packed KV cache with FP8 or NVFP4 latents and MXFP4 index keys, token-sharded prefill, decode context parallelism, and fused low-latency decode.

items.title: Day 0 support for Mistral Large 4 on vLLM
items.description: Day-0 vLLM support for Mistral Large 4 with sparse MLA, cross-layer KV sharing, DSpark speculative decoding, DCP/PCP long context and NIXL P/D on NVIDIA Blackwell.

items.title: Serving DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash at Scale: vLLM Matches DeepInfer and Scales to GB300 NVL72
items.description: With P/D disaggregation and Wide-EP on a GB300 NVL72 rack, vLLM serves DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash on SemiAnalysis AgentX at 954K tokens/s per GPU at a P90 of 196 tokens/s per user, 7.9x our aggregated single-node result.

items.title: GLM-5.3 Optimizations, Part 2: PCP, DCP, and Hybrid HiSparse on 16 H200s
items.description: vLLM serves GLM-5.3 on 16 H200s with PCP and DCP prefill and Hybrid HiSparse decode, reaching 1M-token contexts and 1.7–3.2× the per-user speed of data-parallel P/D on the AgentX agentic benchmark.

items.title: vLLM Delivers Day-0 Support for MiniMax-M3.1-Flash
items.description: Day-0 vLLM support for MiniMax-M3.1-Flash on NVIDIA Blackwell, NVIDIA Rubin, and AMD MI350-series GPUs, with NVFP4 MSA kernels, NVFP4 MegaMoE, DSpark speculative decoding, AgentX results, and day-0 RL.

items.title: Day-0 Support for Flint on vLLM
items.description: vLLM supports both Flint checkpoints (40B total, 2.5B active) from day 0, decoding a single request at about 500 tokens/s on one GPU.

items.title: Announcing Humming: Fast, Flexible Kernels for Quantized Inference
items.description: Introducing Humming, a quantized inference kernel library from Ant Group and the vLLM community, with broad GPU and quantization support, dense and MoE performance results, and vLLM integration.
authors: Ant Group and the vLLM Community

items.title: Introducing vLLM TorchTPU
items.description: vllm-torchtpu is a new vLLM backend for Google Cloud TPUs built on TorchTPU, with Pallas kernels, multi-host parallelism, KV cache offloading, and disaggregated serving.

items.title: Achieving near-zero-downtime scaling in Elastic Expert Parallelism
items.description: How asynchronous preparation and NIXL EP enabled near-zero-downtime Elastic EP scaling in vLLM.

items.title: Hyper Optimizing Kimi K3 in vLLM: Moving Fast and Responsibly
items.description: How agent-assisted CuTe DSL optimizations accelerate Kimi K3 decode on NVIDIA GB300, and how scoped changes, correctness tests, and reproducible benchmarks help ship them responsibly.

items.title: Scaling Kimi K3 on AMD Instinct MI355X: Matching NVIDIA HGX B300 Throughput per GPU on AgentX
items.description: Inside the Kimi K3 optimization effort: understanding the bottlenecks and the decisions that made inference faster

items.title: Serving Reflection Beam on vLLM from Day 0
items.description: vLLM supports Reflection's Beam-1.0 (501B total, 23B active) from day 0, with agent-driven optimization that cut decode latency 2.71× and DFlash2 speculative decoding with adaptive verification.

items.title: Day 0 support for Muse Spark Open on vLLM
items.description: Day-0 vLLM support for Muse Spark Open: 816B MoE, 1M context, multimodal inputs, DSpark speculative decoding, NVIDIA and AMD serving, initial TPU support, and LoRA RL.

items.title: Announcing Day 0 Support for NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Super VL on vLLM
items.description: Run NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Super VL on vLLM for multimodal agent workflows with image, document, and video understanding, OpenAI-compatible serving, and multi-token prediction.

items.title: Adaptive Verification Without a Confidence Head
items.description: An online-fitted acceptance estimator that lets every draft-model speculator use Adaptive Verification, by predicting the target's acceptance probability from the drafter's own logits and refitting continuously during serving.

items.title: Push-Based KV Transfer to Improve TTFT and TPOT for Disaggregated Inference in vLLM
items.description: A push-based NIXL connector for vLLM disaggregated serving: the prefill instance writes KV directly into decode memory over RDMA, taking the router relay, decode-side allocation, and transfer setup off the TTFT critical path.

items.title: Zugwise: Domain-Aware Game Reconstruction for Digitizing Handwritten Chess Scoresheets
items.description: Digitizing handwritten chess scoresheets has been studied as a handwriting-recognition problem: read the move in each box and check that it is legal. This framing misses the errors that matter most. A misread that yields an illegal move is loud. One that yields a legal-but-wrong move is silent, because a legality-only pipeline accepts it and reads every later move against a wrong position. We therefore treat the task as game reconstruction and present Zugwise, which repurposes computer-chess machinery (quiescence search, static exchange evaluation, pin detection) to ask not "what should be played?" but "could a human plausibly have written this?" An absurdity detector makes silent errors loud at or near where they occur, and a backward search traces late symptoms to their cause. Candidate ranking excludes chess-quality signals. A Needleman-Wunsch merge adds the second player's sheet as evidence, and review stops send every disagreement between the sheets' legal readings to a human. In oracle replay of two tournament sections, a release adding them cuts silent errors from 16 to 1 and from 50 to 13. Two learned signals, CTC re-scoring against the recognizer's raw output and a Maia-style human-move prior, raise the correct fix's top-rank rate from 58.8% to 78.0% of the replacement decisions where it is a candidate, and hold without refitting on a later section. On the first section, the human-verified output matches an independent expert transcription move for move on 34 of 45 games, and adjudication against the sheets found errors in both records, on different plies. We do not establish that either workflow is faster or more accurate. The system runs entirely in the browser and is free, private, and offline-capable; alongside it we offer a three-way adjudication protocol for a domain where no single record is ground truth.

items.title: Cleaning an Agent's History Hurts When the World Still Holds the Error
items.description: Tool-using language-model agents accumulate histories of their own mistakes, and a system that compacts, repairs or hands off such a history decides what it says about those mistakes while their effects stay in the world. Prior work cleans the history at a fixed world, where showing a corrected step and saying it is done move together. We ask whether the same correct content helps or hurts depending on how the history states it and what the world holds. We freeze an agent mid-task with its exact world state, edit the history or the world, and let a receiver model continue. On AgentCE-Bench, after the agent commits a wrong value, we hold the world fixed and add the correct value by two natural edits: a truthful note beside the preserved error or the agent's own completed action. The note raises recovery, the share of remaining targets the receiver gets right, from 51% under a matched neutral note to 66%. The completed action lowers it below the unedited history, from 50% to 44%, so the value's presence alone does not predict the effect. On AppWorld, after a database write, we vary whether its receipt reports success or failure and whether its effect is present. A success receipt lowers whole-task success from 45% to 28% while the effect is absent and raises it from 38% to 49% once present. The two effects differ by 27 points pooled over two receivers, a difference positive in six of eight receivers at 97.5% and seven at 95%. A history edit's effect thus depends on the world it describes, and a history made to look clean while the world still holds the error can leave an agent worse off than no edit at all.

items.title: Together Compiler: Continual Compilation for AI Inference
items.description: Today's AI workloads are rapidly changing: new models are released more often, model architectures are increasingly diverse, and traffic distributions change frequently. The challenge we face at Together AI is continual optimization for these changing workloads. Compiling a deployment into an optimized forward pass is a challenge that is well-suited for agent hill-climbing. Existing systems struggle with continual compilation due to a tradeoff between measurement throughput and fidelity. Many systems use agents to optimize individual kernels from the inference forward pass using offline benchmarks, but timings are low-fidelity because of data-dependent behavior in primitives like mixture-of-experts (MoE). On the other hand, systems use agents to directly optimize end-to-end engines but suffer from slow engine launch times. To address these challenges, we build Together Compiler (TKCC), the first truly continual agent loop designed for AI inference optimization. To address the throughput-fidelity tradeoff, we propose: (1) a Tiered Persistent Engine that decouples engine launch overheads from forward pass computation; (2) a cost model to select the parallelism configurations that seed the optimization process. We also conduct extensive ablations on agent context management and present our insights on deploying TKCC in production. TKCC outperforms highly-optimized hand-written Megakernels on the Llama 1B workhorse workload by up to 1.7x and the best open source engines on the latest frontier models (Kimi K3, GLM 5.3, MiniMax M3.1 Flash, DeepSeek v4.1 Flash) across hardware platforms by up to 2.6x higher TPS on the InferenceX benchmark. TKCC also sets the state-of-the-art performance at batch size 1, with 1111 TPS on M3.1 Flash and 1205 TPS on DeepSeek v4.1 Flash. Finally, TKCC generalizes beyond frontier language model inference. TKCC serves trillions of tokens across our production fleet.

items.title: When Should Semantic Priors Enter Partially-Identified Causal Discovery?
items.description: Observational causal discovery often leaves causal di- rections unresolved or unstable. Large language mod- els (LLMs) can provide semantic information to resolve these directions, but incorrect proposals can exclude the true causal graph and invalidate downstream inference. We study three separate decisions: where to allocate semantic queries, which proposals to admit, and which causal graphs to retain.
